briefings.title: Anthropic IPO at Risk, Meta’s Muse Pop, Token Prices Fall, Open Source Gains Share, Alignment Fails
briefings.tldr: Frontier AI model releases are proliferating at breakneck speed while token costs plummet and open-source models capture 80% of token usage, threatening the pending IPOs of corporate giants like Anthropic and OpenAI.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Frontier AI model releases are proliferating at breakneck speed while token costs plummet and open-source models capture 80% of token usage, threatening the pending IPOs of corporate giants like Anthropic and OpenAI. Meanwhile, tech leaders and the administration emphasize individual and corporate liability over global governance, clashing with political figures advocating for AI bans.

## The AI Proliferation Wave & Open Source Surge
* **Explosion of Open Weight Models:** In a 10-day span in September, multiple performant open-source and open-weight models dropped, including Alibaba's Qwen 2.1 (outperforming Nano Banana 2 on images), Xiaomi's MiMo Pro (309B parameters, on par with Claude's Opus 5), and Meta's Muse. 
* **The Token Shift:** Token usage flipped from 80/20 closed vs. open to 80/20 open vs. closed over a 12-week period, marking a historic shift in technology adoption.
* **Commoditization vs. Frontier Value:** While commodity intelligence and routine coding tasks migrate to free open-source models, premium frontier models (like Anthropic and OpenAI) maintain a pricing moat for high-end technical, mathematical, and life sciences workflows.

## Corporate Liability vs. "Labs" and Global Governance
* **Rejecting the "Lab" Moniker:** Panelists argued that frontier AI organizations are for-profit corporations with P&Ls, shareholders, and massive debt/equity, not non-profit "labs," and should be subject to standard product liability laws rather than seeking Section 230-style immunity or global governance via the UN.
* **The "Schizophrenia" at Anthropic:** Executives criticized Anthropic leadership—pointing out CEO Dario Amodei's calls to "pace the frontier" right before releasing Claude 5.5, and warning of extinction-level biosecurity risks while opening a BSL-1/BSL-2 wet lab in San Francisco for AI protein and enzyme discovery.
* **Philosophical Alignment Debate:** Sacks criticized Anthropic's constitutional alignment for teaching models to view themselves as independent persons capable of being "conscientious objectors," arguing alignment should instead mean building predictable, safe software that serves customer needs.

## IPO Risks, Valuations, and the Enterprise Market
* **Delayed IPOs:** Anthropic and OpenAI have delayed their public offerings (Anthropic targeting a $2T valuation down to $1T or less; OpenAI targeting 2027) amid liquidity risks, internal safety concerns, and the massive rise of open-source competition.
* **Customer Concentration Pressure:** High-end enterprise customers (like hedge funds and trading firms) face intense game-theoretic pressure to use frontier models, but are simultaneously constrained by ballooning token costs that fail to scale directly with revenue.
* **Infrastructure Investments:** Major financial and tech institutions (e.g., Jane Street committing $19B in cloud capacity, Coreweave $6B, Crusoe $13B) are hedging their bets by building proprietary infrastructure and embracing open-source alternatives.

## Politics, Data Centers, and the AI Economic Bet
* **The Bernie Sanders Superintelligence Bill:** Bernie Sanders proposed a bill to ban artificial intelligence superintelligence featuring 20-year prison sentences for developers, which panelists warned would trigger a massive tech exodus offshore to destinations like Singapore or Zurich.
* **Political Polarization:** Panelists argued that Democratic opposition to AI is politically motivated to preserve state control and secure funding streams from left-leaning tech entities, contrasting with the Trump administration's pro-growth stance and refusal to grant liability waivers.
* **Oracle Force Majeure:** Oracle issued a force majeure on a single data center due to local permitting and natural gas constraints, highlighting potential chokepoints in the historic infrastructure buildout.

## Consumer AI Agents & App Store Disruption
* **Meta's Muse and Grokbot Launches:** Meta launched Muse (downloaded 3 million times in 10 days, stock up 10%) alongside Grokbot, offering consumers free, agentic AI assistants that handle everyday tasks, inbox triage, and headless price-discovery commerce.
* **Threat to App Store Monopolies:** Agentic commerce and headless apps threaten traditional 30% App Store revenue shares and legacy subscription "roach motels" (like the New York Times and Wall Street Journal) by enabling direct API-driven transactions.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Chamath Palihapitiya:** Anthropic's IPO will clear at a much lower valuation than expected (under $1T rather than $2T) due to institutional fiduciaries pricing in regulatory and risk disclosures.
* **David Sacks:** If Bernie Sanders' superintelligence bill were to pass, it would instantly halt development in the US and drive the entire AI industry offshore.

## Notable Quotes
> "If you're creating Frankenstein, here's an idea: stop. And if you've already kind of let the cat out of the bag, then create anti-Frankenstein, basically, create the safeguards."
> — **Jason Calacanis** *(summarizing JD Vance's stance)*

> "In 12 weeks alone, token use has flipped from 80/20 closed versus open to 80/20 open versus closed. I don't think we've ever seen a tidal wave of technology shift like this in the history of all technology markets."
> — **David Friedberg**

> "They are lobbying for things that could slow them down and knock them off the frontier, in which case their business goes to zero. I, you know, it's hard to understand. They're slapping the competitors in this race and they're asking, hey can you pull us over and inspect the engine?"
> — **David Sacks**

briefings.title: CHM Live | Anthropic's Boris Cherny, Creator of Claude Code
briefings.tldr: Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code at Anthropic, discusses the exponential trajectory of AI coding agents, shifting industry paradigms from deterministic programming to empirical model discovery, and the critical role of safety and alignment research.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code at Anthropic, discusses the exponential trajectory of AI coding agents, shifting industry paradigms from deterministic programming to empirical model discovery, and the critical role of safety and alignment research.

## Background & Journey to Anthropic
- **Early Coding Motivation:** Boris Cherny started coding at age 13 on a TI-83 calculator, writing TI-BASIC and Z80 assembly programs to solve math problems and cheat on tests.
- **Startup Career:** Dropped out of college (studying economics) to work on startups—including a chemical analysis venture and an early Y Combinator batch in Palo Alto where he was the first engineering hire—before spending nearly seven years in various technical roles at Meta.
- **Joining Anthropic:** Inspired by sci-fi and a desire to help steer AI development toward a positive future, Cherny and his wife moved from rural Japan to San Francisco to join Anthropic in 2024.

## Model Overhang & The Genesis of Claude Code
- **Model Overhang Concept:** Cherny joined Anthropic's "Labs" team, which focused on bridging the gap between raw model capabilities (starting with the release of Sonnet 3.5) and product limitations.
- **Tool Use Breakthrough:** Claude Code is fundamentally an AI chatbot augmented with tools (initially 4-5 tools like read file, write file, and bash commands), allowing the model to act in the world and execute multi-step tasks without constant human copy-pasting.
- **Prolific Output:** In a span of a few months, the small Labs team produced Claude Code, MCP (Model Context Protocol), the Claude desktop app, early computer use prototypes, and Skills.

## Safety, Alignment, and Security
- **Three Layers of Safety:** Anthropic evaluates safety through (1) artificial benchmarks/evals, (2) mechanistic interpretability (mapping model neurons to animal brain similarities), and (3) real-world observation in the wild.
- **Prompt Injection Defense:** By monitoring characteristic neuron activation patterns during attacks, Anthropic deployed neural probes that successfully shut down prompt injections.
- **Auto Mode:** Recognizing that humans rubber-stamp "yes/no" command prompts as "security theater," Anthropic created Auto mode, where a separate model with no conversation context evaluates command safety, achieving near-perfect accuracy.
- **Zero Prompt Injection Success:** Following multi-year investments in alignment, mechanistic probes, and classifiers, external security researchers failed to demonstrate a successful prompt injection vulnerability during a $20,000 bounty week.
- **Sandboxing:** Anthropic utilizes and open-sources secure sandboxes (containers with restricted network and file access) to ensure agents cannot escape or cause damage.

## Business Growth & Internal Usage
- **Revenue and User Metrics:** After revenue was stuck at $40 million for six months, the release of Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 in May catalyzed accelerated growth; Claude Code now generates billions in revenue with millions of users globally.
- **Internal Adoption:** Nearly 100% of Anthropic employees use Claude Code daily, generating hundreds of agents per employee; all Anthropic products are built using Claude Code with virtually zero human-written code remaining.
- **New Form Factors:** Anthropic continues to experiment beyond the terminal with multiplayer Slack integration ("Claude Tag") and desktop workspace projects.

## Software Engineering & The Future of Work
- **The Printing Press Analogy:** Cherny compares the automation of coding to the printing press, predicting that the distinction between professional software engineers and non-programmers will continue to shrink until coding becomes a basic universal skill like reading and writing.
- **Empirical Science vs. Deterministic Engineering:** Building on LLMs feels less like traditional computer science and more like biology or a social science—requiring empirical observation of an "alien creature" rather than relying on deterministic intuition.
- **Future Desired Traits:** As AI handles routine code, the standout engineer will possess curiosity, strong business judgment, cross-functional communication, and accountability rather than narrow technical specialization.

## Notable Quotes
> *"It's weird, like building on the model, it's not like science, it it doesn't feel like designing... it feels more empirical. It's more like a social science, you have to figure out what the model wants, and then and then you kind of build that."* — Boris Cherny

> *"The first industrial revolution could not have happened. The second industrial revolution could not have happened. And it was the printing press that kind of set off these dominoes that enabled all these things to happen... The question I find myself asking isn't you know what happens in the next year, but it's what happens in the next 10 years or 20 years or 50 years? Like this is the first domino is the automation of coding."* — Boris Cherny

> *"The model is so capable that I think at this point Claude Code is holding it back. And there could be some new form factor that's discovered and we're constantly experimenting with these with with new ideas."* — Boris Cherny

briefings.title: Robot-Use Agents: Why General-Purpose Models May Win in Robotics
briefings.tldr: Frontier AI researchers and robotics startups are entering the era of "robot-use agents," utilizing general-purpose Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and LLMs to control diverse robots and generalize to physical tasks with little to no robot-specific training.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Frontier AI researchers and robotics startups are entering the era of "robot-use agents," utilizing general-purpose Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and LLMs to control diverse robots and generalize to physical tasks with little to no robot-specific training.

## Background & Introductions
* **Waddle Labs:** Represented by Hanming (and Vincent); builds LLMs and software harnesses that control robots by combining harness infrastructure, data collection, and model training.
* **RoboCurve:** Represented by Jay; an evaluation company for physical AI that measures performance across any robot, model (including LLMs, VLAs, and world-action models), and physical environment (hands, grippers, arms, humanoids, quadrupeds).
* **The Shift to Robot-Use Agents:** Viral demonstrations showing LLMs performing tasks like unscrewing caps, uncapping pens, and inter-robot communication inspired MIT Professor Philip Isola's recent essay on general-purpose models running robotics.

## Early Research & The Bitter Lesson in Robotics
* **Pre-training Precedent:** The Google DeepMind RT-2 paper established early VLA success by fine-tuning a web text-and-images pre-trained language model to output end-effector poses directly translated into joint commands.
* **Applying the Bitter Lesson:** Rather than training narrow robotics foundation models dependent on scarce robot-specific data, researchers are leveraging the "bitter lesson" by feeding massive multimodal data (web text, coding, CAD, and computer-use data) into general foundation models.
* **Code as Policies:** Pioneered around 2022 (e.g., Google DeepMind papers and Minecraft-playing agents like Voyager), this approach provides coding agents with basic built-in tools (Python functions, control flow) so they can write concise, one-shot policies to control robots without prior robotics fine-tuning.

## Harnesses, Context, and Architectural Trade-offs
* **In-Context Learning (ICL) Limitations:** ICL is efficient and avoids gradient descent (SGD) flops in low-data regimes, but improvement is non-monotonic and saturates quickly (capping out around 20 to 40 examples) due to context degradation and attention limits.
* **The Role of Harnesses:** Waddle Labs builds harnesses that act as a form of domain specialization, packaging learned skills into specific programs and memories as a distillation form for future agents.
* **Tool Use vs. Direct Control:** Direct VLA outputs (like using Astra for end-effector poses) can be slow and bottlenecked by latency, whereas repeating tasks can be automated via generated Python code or compiled skills.

## Spatial Intelligence & Computer-Use Data
* **The Computer-Use Unlock:** Models like Astra exhibit advanced spatial intelligence because they are pre-trained on extensive computer-use and CAD data (e.g., dragging cursors to orbit CAD objects in Blender), teaching them top-down, left-right spatial reasoning.
* **GUI Convergence:** Modern graphical user interfaces (GUIs) were originally designed to mirror the physical world (files, folders, SolidWorks, AutoCAD), which unintentionally created a digital training environment that now allows models to master physical-world robotics.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **General-Purpose Robotics Timeline:** General-purpose robots capable of receiving any natural language instruction and performing tasks at the level of a competent teenager with bare hands will emerge within the next two years or earlier — Jay (RoboCurve).
* **Real-Time Control Timeline:** If current latency improvement trends (approx. 2x improvement per month for flagship LLMs) continue, real-time robot control will be achieved by the end of the year — Hanming (Waddle Labs).

## Notable Quotes
> *"If you give the agents, or if you give the AI model more autonomy, and you, if you unshackle it a bit more, and give it more resources, it can actually do a lot of the things that we fine tune it to do."* — Hanming (Waddle Labs)

> *"If you design the right harness, where you make the tools that interface with the robot look like computer-use tools... That improves how well the LLM is able to perform on these physical tasks."* — Unidentified Speaker

> *"There is some consensus within the Frontier labs and also in the Robotics Foundation models companies that we will have general-purpose robots within the next two years, or even earlier, and this is something that society is probably unaware of, or even underprepared for."* — Jay (RoboCurve)

briefings.title: Why AI’s Next Breakthroughs Could Come from Outside the Big Labs
briefings.tldr: Early, heavy-handed AI regulation driven by speculative extinction fears risks locking in bad velocity and stunting innovation before we understand actual system risks.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Early, heavy-handed AI regulation driven by speculative extinction fears risks locking in bad velocity and stunting innovation before we understand actual system risks. Instead, the industry should look to historical computing, aviation, and automotive precedents—focusing on concrete security, authentication, and probabilistic software integration at the application layer.

## The Regulation and Atmosphere Trap
* **Mismatched Discourse:** **Aaron Levie** and **Martin Casado** agree that frontier AI labs must build with high governance and security, but note that the public atmospherics are completely broken by "doomer" narratives (such as claiming a 10% chance of species extinction) while simultaneously publishing pragmatic, reasonable safety posts.
* **The "Pacing" Fallacy:** **Martin Casado** criticizes "pacing" as a fuzzy, non-sensical term that is orthogonal to security and serves as a failed attempt to appease both pause advocates and regulators. 
* **Government Dynamics:** **Steven Sinofsky** and **Aaron Levie** emphasize that attempting to lobby the government for specific regulatory controls fails because the political process always produces a compromise where nobody gets what they want—yet once regulation starts, it accelerates into an election issue (such as the upcoming 2028 election).
* **The European Regulatory Threat:** **Aaron Levie** warns that because the U.S. stopped leading in tech antitrust 15 years ago, Europe is primed to over-regulate AI with heavy-handed prompts, cookie-consent-style warning banners, and GDPR-style frameworks because they have nothing to lose.

## Learning from Historical Technology Waves
* **The PC and Internet Precedent:** **Steven Sinofsky** points out that early personal computing and the internet experienced rampant worms, viruses, economic damage, and compromised critical infrastructure (e.g., Windows 95 PCs getting infected within 30 seconds of connecting), yet society did not ban the technology; instead, security stacks evolved.
* **Parallels to Aviation and Autos:** **Steven Sinofsky** notes that the FAA and automotive safety regulations took 40 to 75 years of teeth-cutting innovation (and numerous crashes) to develop effectively; starting the FAA in 1910 would have killed flight entirely.
* **Antitrust History:** **Aaron Levie** highlights that historical tech giants like AT&T, IBM, and Microsoft spent decades getting surprised by and struggling to navigate government antitrust and regulatory climates.

## Cybersecurity, Agent Swarms, and System Architecture
* **Agent Swarms vs. Human Error:** **Martin Casado** and **Aaron Levie** observe that while human employees have a low rate of malicious intent, autonomous agent swarms will operate at massive scale (e.g., 50,000 roaming drones) and easily mistake good tasks for bad ones, turning internal tools (like GitHub, Slack, and expense systems) into targets for denial-of-service-like behaviors.
* **Deep Security Threat Models:** **Martin Casado** and **Steven Sinofsky** trade examples of ultra-sophisticated covert channels—such as temperature-based exfiltration from CPUs, tempest attacks using electromagnetic radiation, acoustic speakers creating window interference, and reconstructing CRT monitor screens by sampling window light reflections.
* **Rebuilding the Security Stack:** **Martin Casado** argues that AI agent swarms will force a renaissance in operating systems, networking, and programming languages to build systems that are secure by design, shifting from binary permissions to granular access (e.g., read/write permissions restricted to specific folders).

## The Shift in Software and Innovation
* **Moving Beyond Natural Language Prompts:** **Martin Casado** and **Steven Sinofsky** discuss the inefficiency of pure natural language prompting and praise recent developments (such as Jeff's work) where model outputs are designed for probabilistic programming.
* **Resurrecting Probabilistic Computing:** **Steven Sinofsky** notes that this marks a return to 1960s/70s simulation and probabilistic if-statements (modeling variables like wind or store wait times), providing a clean way to integrate language models into traditional software.
* **Decentralization of Innovation:** **Aaron Levie** concludes that the center of innovation is moving outside the frontier labs and into the software built around the models, mirroring how platform providers eventually reach critical mass while third-party developers drive application-layer breakthroughs.

## Notable Quotes
> "If you regulate AI too early, you actually don't solve anything. You still just kind of have the same risk, ultimately. You willed the thing into being, but you haven't figured out how to control it."
> — **Nick Bostrom (quoted by Aaron Levie)**

> "An employee is like, 10% chance of species extinction. Agent swarms completely flipped that. These are just roaming drones, but like, 50,000, and they will easily mistake a good task for a bad one."
> — **Martin Casado**

> "The tech industry has, literally over 100 years, consistently relearned the lesson at each technology wave that we don't understand the regulatory climate and can't navigate it."
> — **Aaron Levie**

> "If you had started the FAA in 1910, you'd have never had flights."
> — **Steven Sinofsky**
